title: Apple TV packs November with comedy, heist thriller and Oscar follow-up
text:
Apple TV packs November with comedy, heist thriller and Oscar follow-up | LavX News Skip to content LavX News Trends Regulation Business Startups Hardware Chips Laptops Smartphones Cloud DevOps Serverless Infrastructure Security Vulnerabilities Privacy Cybersecurity Dev Python Rust Mobile Backend Frontend AI Robotics LLMs Machine Learning Bookmarks Sign In English Sign In # Business Apple TV packs November with comedy, heist thriller and Oscar follow-up
 Oct 23, 2026, 4:46 PM UTC • Tomáš Novák • 2 min read Share this article Save Apple TV releases "Stick" season 2, the heist drama "12 12 12," and Siân Heder’s "Being Heumann" in November, plus new episodes for "Brothers," "Nocturne," and others.
 Apple TV packs November with a comedy sequel, a heist thriller, an Oscar-winning director’s follow-up, and new episodes across several series. The lineup spans sports comedy, culinary docuseries, disability rights drama, and holiday specials. 
 "Stick" (season 2) arrives Nov. 4. Owen Wilson plays Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill ex-pro golfer whose career collapsed two decades ago. After his marriage fails and he takes a job at an Indiana sporting goods store, he bets everything on Santi, a troubled 17-year-old golf phenom played by Peter Dager. The comedy places found-family dynamics inside golf culture. 
 "Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook" debuts Nov. 6. Nora Lum, a Hollywood actor and comedian, descends from restaurant royalty but cannot cook. She travels on a culinary road trip to revive her family’s beloved Chinese eatery. 
 "12 12 12" starts Nov. 13. Each episode unfolds across three timelines: 12 months of planning, 12 hours of the heist, and 12 days after. Anthony Mackie plays a disgraced FBI agent; Jamie Dornan plays an American career criminal. They chase each other across Europe, centering on a vault raid beneath Zurich’s streets.
 "Being Heumann" also lands Nov. 13. Ruth Madeley plays Judy Heumann, a disabled woman who, in 1977, joins a coalition to occupy a federal building. The occupation becomes the longest in American history, forcing bureaucrats to act. Siân Heder, who won an Oscar for "CODA," directs the drama based on true events.
 "Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy" arrives Nov. 13. Snoopy lands on Santa’s naughty list with 12 days until Christmas. He sets out to prove he is not a bad beagle, discovering that the season means more than gifts.
 "Way of the Warrior Kid" releases Nov. 25. Jude Hill plays Marc, a middle schooler bullied by classmates. His injured uncle Jake, a decorated Navy SEAL played by Chris Pratt, spends the summer with Marc and his mother Sarah, played by Linda Cardellini. Jake devises "Operation Warrior Kid" to teach Marc courage rather than fighting. McG directs from a screenplay by Will Staples, based on Jocko Willink’s novel.
 Apple TV rolls out new episodes for ongoing series. "Brothers," starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, continues through Nov. 4. "Small Prophets" continues through Nov. 4. "Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars" continues through Nov. 6. "Where’s Wanda?" continues through Dec. 9. "Nocturne," starring Liev Schreiber, continues through Dec. 25.
 Apple TV costs $14.99 per month, or subscribers can bundle it through Apple One. Visit Apple TV+ for details.

 The AI Dividend Has Not Reached Mainstream Corporate America
 Despite massive investment and widespread adoption rhetoric, artificial intelligence has produced no measurable financial payoff outside the technology sector.  Amazon scraps four Loudoun data centers, turns site into housing and community space
 Amazon canceled plans for four data centers on a 122-acre former university campus in Loudoun County, Virginia, after residents objected to noise and power demands. The company will donate 25 acres for community use and contribute $5 million to local housing funds.
 Schwarzman addresses BlackRock confusion in 23rd Nikkei column
 Blackstone Chairman Stephen Schwarzman used the 23rd installment of his Nikkei Asia personal history series to examine the persistent naming confusion with BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager led by Larry Fink. The column traces the shared corporate origins and the strategic split that created two distinct financial empires.
